item.research_question: Can the nature and extent of local chemical ordering in high-entropy alloys be systematically controlled using binary enthalpies of mixing to enhance mechanical properties while overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off?
item.material_system: FCC CoFeNi base alloy with controlled additions of Al and Ti (CoFeNi, Al0.25CoFeNi, Al0.3CoFeNi, Al0.3Ti0.2CoFeNi) and BCC NbTaTi base alloy with Al addition (NbTaTi, Al0.5NbTaTi)
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc melting followed by homogenization and solution treatment at 1,200 °C (1 h for FCC ingots, 48 h for BCC ingots), cold rolling (50% reduction for FCC), annealing at 1,200 °C for 5 min, and water quenching; subsequent isothermal annealing at 500 °C for 0 to 5 h for ordering evolution studies
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 0.001/s for FCC alloys; room temperature compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001/s for BCC alloys
key_findings: Yield strength of the near-random CoFeNi alloy was 181 MPa, increasing to 802 MPa in the Al0.3Ti0.2CoFeNi alloy with well-developed long-range order.
Tensile ductility increased from ~21% for the random CoFeNi alloy to ~76% for the Al0.3CoFeNi alloy containing early-stage long-range ordered domains.
The Al0.25CoFeNi alloy exhibited short-range ordered Ni–Al-rich clusters with an average diameter of 3 ± 1.5 nm and a yield strength of 287 MPa.
The Al0.3CoFeNi alloy showed early-stage long-range order domains of 3 ± 1.5 nm size with a yield strength of 454 MPa.
The Al0.3Ti0.2CoFeNi alloy displayed well-developed long-range ordered domains of ~8 ± 2 nm size.
In the BCC system, the Al0.5NbTaTi alloy showed a yield stress of ~1,039 MPa compared to ~587 MPa for the base NbTaTi alloy, while maintaining ~52% compressive plastic strain.
DFT calculations indicated that short-range ordering in Al0.27CoFeNi reduces total energy by 0.118 to 0.200 eV per Al atom at 1,200 °C.
Solid solution strengthening was calculated to contribute only 20 to 30 MPa, confirming that chemical ordering is the primary driver for the observed strength increase.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that controlled additions of elements with large negative binary enthalpies of mixing (Al, Ti) drive the formation of short-range ordered (SRO) domains and long-range ordered (LRO) precipitates (L12 in FCC, B2 in BCC). These nanoscale ordered domains act as obstacles to dislocation motion, significantly boosting yield strength. The simultaneous increase in ductility is attributed to a deformation mechanism involving glide plane softening, localized slip in multiple {111} planes, and a dynamic Hall–Petch-like effect that refines slip length and triggers homogeneous dislocation-mediated plasticity.
item.limitations: The study notes that the thermodynamic framework relies on binary enthalpies of mixing and assumes similar vibrational entropic contributions; the authors state that future studies will include vibrational entropy effects to improve accuracy. Additionally, the BCC system validation was limited to preliminary compression tests.
item.future_work: The authors propose that future studies will include the effects of vibrational entropy to improve the accuracy of computational results and that the detailed microscopy and fundamental deformation mechanisms of these alloys are subjects of future interest.
quotes: Specifically, a progressively increasing local order boosts the tensile yield strengths of the parent CoFeNi alloy by a factor of four while also substantially improving ductility, which breaks the so-called strength–ductility paradox.

Our hypothesis was tested via detailed investigations in four different alloys—CoFeNi (33Co-33Fe-33Ni at.%), Al0.25CoFeNi (7.6Al-30.8Co-30.8Fe-30.8Ni at.%), Al0.3CoFeNi (9.1Al-30.3Co-30.3Fe-30.3Ni at.%), and Al0.3Ti0.2CoFeNi (8.5Al-5.7Ti-28.6Co-28.6Fe-28.6Ni at.%).

The simultaneous increase in strength and ductility from CoFeNi to Al0.25CoFeNi to Al0.3CoFeNi shown here suggests that this bottleneck may be overcome by introducing ordering (SRO or early-stage LRO) within the solid solution matrix of HEAs.
